decision_notes: Each decision follows the same pattern: what we chose, why, and what it costs. Reviewers judge trade-offs, not just choices.
I gave 'When to revisit' its own heading instead of burying it in the Redis paragraph. That way a future reader scanning for scaling concerns finds it directly.
I rejected a bullet list mirroring the notes. Bullets would drop the 'because' reasoning that makes the section worth reading.
Assumption to check: '~6 upstream calls per city per hour' assumes every city is requested at least every 10 minutes. That holds at 40 req/min, but confirm the 12 cities really dominate traffic.
prediction_prompt: If a reviewer sees only 'TTL: 10 minutes' with no explanation, what question do you predict they'll ask? Which sentence in the draft pre-empts it?
draft:
## Design decisions

**Why a cache at all.** The forecast API was receiving ~40 requests/min, almost all for the same 12 cities. Caching responses removes nearly all of that redundant upstream traffic.

**TTL: 10 minutes.** Upstream forecasts change only hourly, so a longer TTL would usually be safe. We chose 10 minutes so that users see a new forecast within 10 minutes of an upstream update, not up to an hour later. The cost is about 6 upstream calls per city per hour, which is negligible.

**In-process LRU (256 entries), not Redis.**
[[GAP gap-1]]
We run a single instance, so a shared cache buys us nothing yet. Redis would add another service to deploy, monitor, and keep available. An in-process LRU has no network hop and no new dependency, and 256 entries covers our 12 cities with plenty of headroom.
[[/GAP]]

**Serve stale on upstream errors.** If the upstream call fails and we hold an expired entry, we return it marked as stale instead of returning an error. A slightly old forecast is more useful than none, and the stale flag lets clients decide how to display it.

**When to revisit.** Past one instance, each instance would hold its own cache. That multiplies upstream calls and lets instances serve inconsistent data. At that point, move to Redis or another shared cache.

gaps.description: Write 2-3 sentences justifying an in-process LRU over Redis. Cover why the alternative isn't needed now, what it would cost us, and why 256 entries is enough.
gaps.hint: A good rationale names the condition that makes the rejected option unnecessary *today*. Look at the notes for the one fact about our deployment that makes a shared cache pointless.

takeaway: Design rationale earns its place by stating the alternative you rejected, the reason it doesn't fit now, and the condition under which you'd change your mind.
